new_statements.quote: Two independent descriptions of Mien (Downer 1961, Purnell 1965) and a note on Mun in Shintani and Yang (1990) show these two vowel length languages are characterized by a prosody that alternates short and long (or light and heavy) syllables. Downer (1961:539) describes Mien (“Highland Yao”) as follows: “[Reduced syllables] ... agree in having weaker stress and shorter duration than the following full syllables so that a strong iambic rhythm is imparted to disyllabic words …”. Given the iambic rhythm of these languages, not only must non-phrase-final syllables be light, but phrase-final syllables (syntactic heads) must maintain a certain gravity.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. Opened (310 pp, text layer). Printed p. 28 (PDF p. 39): the passage is there as point "4)" of §2.1.3.2. Only difference: the reader's quote elides one sentence inside Downer's quotation with "...": the PDF reads "[Reduced syllables] are of two kinds—regular reduced syllables, and reduced syllables in -a. The two kinds agree in having weaker stress and shorter duration than the following full syllables so that a strong iambic rhythm is imparted to disyllabic words …". Fn. 18 (135 Shintani & Yang sentences, vowel length correlates with phrase-final position) is on the same page. p. 199 (PDF p. 212), §4.2.1: "They are unstressed, and in some languages they may harmonize with the n…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kim Mun is an 8-tone language; the only stress-like statement is second-hand: Mien and Mun share an iambic light-heavy prosody in which reduced/minor syllables and nominal prefixes are unstressed and short, and the following full (word/phrase-final) syllable carries the prominence and full tone. Clark 2008 (first-hand, Lao and Vietnam Kim Mun) never mentions stress but describes toneless mid-pitch minor syllables and non-final vowel shortening with tone neutralization, consistent with that picture.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kim Mun; the direct 'weaker stress' wording is Downer's about Iu Mien (Highland Yao), extended to Mun by Ratliff on the strength of a note in Shintani & Yang 1990.
new_statements.domain_note: Ratliff frames it as word/phrase prosody: non-phrase-final syllables light, phrase-final syllables (syntactic heads) heavy; fn. 18 reports Hainan Mun vowel length correlating with phrase-final position. Clark 2008 pp. 83, 117 reports non-word-final vowel shortening and tone neutralization in citation-form compounds.
new_statements.identity_note: Clark 2008 describes 'Lao Kim Mun' (Lantien/Lanten of Luang Namtha, Laos) and 'Vietnam Kim Mun' (Lao Cai); Ratliff's second-hand note concerns Hainan Mun (Shintani & Yang 1990). All fall under kimm1245 (Glottolog lists no dialect children). Downer 1961 and Purnell 1965, quoted by Ratliff, describe Iu Mien (iumi1238), not Kim Mun.

sources.note: Silent on stress: the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur anywhere in the thesis. Both varieties have 8 tones (5.1.3, 6.1.3); word structure (C.)C1(C2)V(C3)T with optional word-initial minor (pre-)syllable that has 'no distinctive tone', a shortened schwa, and 'pitch level... of about mid range' (p. 91; Vietnam variety 'do not carry tone', p. 125); non-word-final syllables show vowel shortening and Shintani-style 'tone neutralization where only the target pitch level is produced' (p. 83; p. 117).
